ANNALINGAM PREMASHANKER, J.
This is an appeal by LANKA TILES PLC (Hereinafter sometimes referred
to as the Tax Payer/Appellant) from the determination of the Tax Appeals
Commission dated 14.05.2024 made in TAC appeal no.
TAC/IT/103/2018. The Respondent is the Commissioner General of
Inland Revenue (Hereinafter sometimes referred to as the CGIR/
Respondent). The Appellant is a company incorporated and domiciled in
Sri Lanka and is engaged in the manufacture and sale of glazed ceramic
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 3|16
and porcelain floor tiles. The Tax in dispute 54,559, 770. 00, penalty 22,
The Appellant being dissatisfied with the Determination of Tax Appeals
Commission (Hereinafter sometimes referred to as TAC) requested for an
appeal by a case stated for the opinion of the Court of Appeal by their
communication dated 18.06.2024.
The tax payer submits its income tax return for the taxable period
2013/2014 with a claim of qualifying payment for the expansion of
undertaking. The claim was rejected by the Assessor and that the Tax
Payer was not entitled for qualifying payment. The return is not accepted
and issued an assessment disallowing the claim. Having aggrieved by the
said Assessments, the tax payer made an appeal to the CGIR. The Tax
Payer made the same agitation before the CGIR. CGIR by his
determination dated 20.03.2018 determined the appeal by confirming the
assessments. The tax payer having not satisfied with the determination
of the CGIR, made an appeal to the TAC. In the appeal before the TAC
the tax payer raised the same issues. TAC by its determination dated
14.05.2024, upheld the determination of the Inland Revenue Department
and dismissed the appeal. Thereafter, the Tax Payer being dissatisfied
with the said determination of the TAC requested TAC by his
communication dated 18.06.2024 to have a case stated for the opinion of
the Court of Appeal.
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 4|16
In the case stated dated 08.07.2024 following questions were raised for
the opinion of the Court of Appeal:-
1. Has the Tax Appeals Commission erred in law in its determination
of the grounds of appeal of the Appellant?
2. Has the Tax Appeals Commission erred in law in failing to apply or
follow binding decisions of the Supreme Court and the Court of
Appeal of Sri Lanka?
3. Whether the Tax Appeals Commission erred in law in determining
that the investment of Rs. 779,425,304/- in the acquisition of
fixed assets by the Appellant is not an expansion of any
undertaking within the meaning of section 34(2) (s) of the Inland
Revenue Act No. 2006 as amended and/ or is not a qualifying
payment as defined in Section 34(2) (s) of the Inland Revenue Act
No. 10 of 2006 as amended?
4. Whether the Tax Appeals Commission erred in law in determining
that there was merely a replacement of an old machine rather
than an expansion of an undertaking?
5. Has the Tax Appeals Commission erred in law in its interpretation
of Section 34(2)(s) of the Inland Revenue Act No.10 of 2006 as
amended in relation to allowance in respect of the qualifying
payment claimed by the Appellant?
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 5|16
6. Has the Tax Appeals Commission erred in law in considering
reasons other than the reasons set out by the Assistant
Commissioner in his communication of the purported reasons for
not accepting the return of the Appellant?
7. Without prejudice to the position that the Tax Appeals
Commission is not entitled consider reasons other than those
communicated by the Assistant Commissioner in writing to the
Appellant in terms of the proviso to section 163(3) for not
accepting the return, has the Tax Appeals Commission erred in
law
a) In relying on decisions of the Committee of
Interpretation of Tax Law of the Inland Revenue
Department in the determination of the IRD?
b) In its interpretation of a new undertaking?
c) In its interpretation of section 16C or 17A in relation to
the qualifying payment claimed by the Appellant?
Questions of Law No. 3, 4, 5 and 7
The above Questions of Law 3, 4, 5, and 7 are on the investment,
expansion of undertaking and on qualifying payment which are related to
each other. Hence, all the above questions of law are dealt together.
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 6|16
The Tax Payer after the end of ethnic conflict in May 2009, decided to
expand its business and thus a total of Rs. 779,425,304 was invested in
the expansion of certain undertaking. In this background for the taxable
period 2013/2014, a claim of Rs. 194,856,326 as a qualifying payment
under section 34(1) and 34(2) of IRA No. 10 of 2006 was made.
Tax Payer received an intimation dated 13.05.2016 and also Notice of
Assessment 30.05.2016 relating to the return of income for the year of
Assessment 2013/2014. The Tax Payer made an appeal to the CGIR.
CGIR confirmed the Assessment by his determination dated 20.03.2018.
The Tax Payer made an appeal to the TAC. TAC confirmed the
Assessment by its determination dated 14.05.2024.
The dispute before this Court arises from the Appellant's claim for a
qualifying payment under section 34(2)(s) of the Inland Revenue Act No.
10 of 2006, as amended. The Appellant had made substantial
investments in fixed assets and claimed a qualifying payment in respect
of such investment. The total investment relied upon by the Appellant
was approximately Rs. 779,425,304/-, and the qualifying payment
claimed was approximately Rs. 194,856,326/-
It is necessary at the outset to consider the statutory provision upon
which the Appellant relies.
Section 34 (1). Subject to the provisions of subsection (4), there
shall be deducted, for the purposes of section 33, from the
assessable income of a person for any year of assessment in
respect of every qualifying payment made by him or deemed to
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 7|16
have been made by him in that year of assessment, an allowance
equal to the amount of such qualifying payment.
(1) In this section, “qualifying payment” means–
(a) a donation made by any person in money to an approved
charity;
(b) a donation made in money or otherwise to–
(i) the Government of Sri Lanka;
(ii) a local authority;
(iii) any Higher Educational Institution established or
deemed to be established under the Universities Act, No.
(iv) the Buddhist and Pali University or any Higher
Educational Institution established by or under the
Buddhist and Pali University Act, No. 74 of 1981;
(v) a fund established by the Government of Sri Lanka,
(vi) a fund established by a local authority and approved
by the Minister ;
(vii) the Sevana Fund created and administered by the
National Housing Development Authority established by
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 8|16
the National Housing Development Authority Act, No. 17
(viii) a fund established by a Provincial Council and
approved by the Minister:
(ix) the Api Wenuwen Api Fund established by Api
Wenuwen Api Fund Act, No. 6 of 2008, (x) National
Kidney Fund established under the National Kidney
Foundation of Sri Lanka (Incorporation) Act, No. 34 of
Provided where the fund referred to in sub-paragraph
(v) of this paragraph is the President’s Fund established
by the President’s Fund Act, No.7 of 1978 and any public
corporation is required in terms of the law by or under
which such corporation is established to remit any
profits of such corporation to the President’s Fund, the
profits so remitted shall be deemed for the purpose of
this paragraph, to be donations made to such Fund;
Provided that such part, if any as is in excess of two
million rupees of any donation made otherwise than in

money, shall be deemed not to comprise a qualifying

(s) investment of not less than fifty million rupees in the
acquisition of fixed assets made by any person on or after
April 1, 2011 but before April 1, 2014 in the expansion of
any undertaking which would have been qualified for
exemption under section 16C or section 17A had such
undertaking commenced to carry on business on or after
Section 34 of the Inland Revenue Act deals with allowances in respect of
qualifying payments. Paragraph (s) of subsection (2), in the form
applicable to the relevant period, provides for an investment of not less
than fifty million rupees in the acquisition of fixed assets made on or
after 1 April 2011 but before 1 April 2015 in the expansion of an
undertaking which would have been qualified for exemption under
section 16C or section 17A had such undertaking commenced to carry
on business on or after 1 April 2011. The provision further contains a
proviso concerning certain high technology plant, machinery or
equipment acquired for specified purposes, including energy efficiency,
technology upgrading, introduction of new technology or power
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 10|16
generation using renewable energy resources, and extending the relevant
period in the circumstances specified therein.
It is therefore clear that section 34(2)(s)has not provided that every
investment in fixed assets exceeding fifty million rupees automatically
constitutes a qualifying payment. The investment must be an investment
in the acquisition of fixed assets, must satisfy the monetary and
temporal requirements of the provision, and, importantly for the present
appeal, must be an investment “in the expansion of any undertaking”
which satisfies the statutory provision incorporated by reference to
sections 16C or 17A.
There are four requirements of section 34(2)(s) of IRA for a claim of
“qualifying payment”. The investment must;
I. Be not less than fifty million rupees,
II. Be made in the course of an acquisition of fixed assets,
III. Be on or after 1st April 2011 but before 1st April 2015,
IV. Be done in the expansion of undertakings.
The investment made in this case is 450 million which is more than fifty
million rupees, this satisfies the first requirement of the fifty million
limit. Then, the investment of 450 million was made for acquisition of a
fixed machinery, this satisfies the second requirement of acquiring fixed
asset. The investment was made in the year of assessment 2013/2014,
this satisfies the third requirement of time period. Therefore, it can be
considered that the payment in this case must satisfy the 4 limbs under
Section 34(2)(s). Since the first three limbs have been satisfied, the fourth
limb of expansion will be discussed further in this case.
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 11|16
Section 34 (2)(s) proviso reads as:
Provided however, where such investment is made in any high
tech plant, machinery or equipment which is acquired for
energy efficiency purposes or for technology upgrading
purposes or introducing any new technology or for power
generation using renewable energy resources in the expansion
of such un dertaking on or after April 1, 2011 but prior to April
1, 2015 such investment shall compromise a qualifying
payment”
The word expansion is not defined in IRA. The Oxford dictionary meaning
is:
“EXPAND – an act of increasing or making something increase in
size, amount or importance”
“The company is expanding growth.”
The word “expansion” is not defined in section 34(2)(s). The ordinary
meaning of the word is enlargement, extension or increase in the size, or
extent of something already existing. The Court must therefore determine
whether, on the facts established before the tax authorities, the
investment made by the Appellant amounted to an enlargement or
extension of its undertaking. In the present case the word which
assumes importance in expansion. The statutory requirement of
expansion is found in the provision itself.
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 12|16
In this case, the Respondent do not challenge or deny that new Kiln is
more efficient and contain new technology and thereby amount to an
upgrading. It will mean that the company that demolished an old factory
and built a new factory will not qualify, as it is a replacement of one
factory with another. The whole objective of the section is to encourage
undertakings to expand their operations, to modernize equipment. This
requirement has been satisfied.
Having granted total exemption to companies which commenced
business operations after April 1, 2011, in the areas of activities referred
to in section 16C(2) and 17A(2) and satisfies the exemption of section
16C or 17A as the case may be, they sought to encourage businesses
which had commenced carrying on such activities prior April 1, 2011 to
expand their existing business undertakings. The legislature, to promote
and develop the activities specified in section 16C(2) and 17A(2), decided
to grant qualifying payments to persons engaging in the referred to in
section 16C or section 17A if they satisfied the requirements of such
sections but had commenced business before 1 April, 2011.
A company which had invested not less than fifty million rupees in fixed
assets made by any person on or after April 1, 2011 but before April 1,
2015 in the expansion of any undertaking who would have been qualified
for exemption under section 16C or section 17A had such undertaking
commenced to carry on business on or after April 1, 2011 was granted a
qualifying payment.
The Appellant submitted that the Tax Appeals Commission erred in law
in determining that the investment of Rs. 779,425,304/- in the
acquisition of fixed assets by the Appellant is not an expansion of any
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 13|16
undertaking within the meaning of section 34(2) (s) of the Inland
Revenue Act No. 10 of 2006 as amended.
It is further submitted by the Appellant that the Tax Appeals
Commission erred in law in determining that the investment of Rs.
779,425,304/- in the acquisition of fixed assets by the Appellant is not a
qualifying payment as defined in section 34(2) (s) of the Inland Revenue
Act No. 10 of 2006 as amended. The TAC erred in law in its
interpretation of Section 34(2) (s) of IRA No. 10 of 2006 as amended in
relation to allowance in respect of the qualifying payment claimed by the
Appellant.
The Tax Payer in its factory, a Kiln – 01 was demolished and a modern
Kiln 04 was installed. The company has invested a lot of sum in the said
project as it is an expansion of the undertaking; they claim to be a
qualifying payment. There is no doubt that the undertaking of the
Appellant has become larger. There is no dispute that turnover of the
Appellant has dramatically increased. There is not dispute installed
capacity of tile production has increased exponentially.
Therefore, the increase in the scope of the activity or the scale of the
operation of the company can be considered as expansion. In this
instance by installing Kiln - 04, the company has increased its products
and etc. Therefore, the company had expansion of undertaking and
entitled for qualifying payment.
As explained above, the Court is answering the Questions of Law No.
3, 4, 5 and 7 (a,b,c) in affirmative.
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 14|16
Questions of Law No. 1, 2, and 6
The above Questions of Law are dealt with reasoning and grounds of
appeal which are related to each other. Hence, the above questions are
dealt together.
In the determination of the CGIR, they have considered the amount of
investment, expansion of undertaking and the increase of the turnover.
From the said determination an appeal was preferred to the TAC. The
grounds of appeal are amount of investment, expansion of undertaking
and the increase of turnover. But in the TAC determination it has been
said that the grounds of appeal are; Amount of investment, Expansion of
undertaking, Increase in turnover and Eligibility of claim of qualifying
payment.
Accordingly, TAC has considered additional grounds of appeal which is in
respect of claim of qualifying payment.
TAC sat on appeal. The appeal is from the determination of the CGIR.
TAC cannot consider new materials which were not before the CGIR for
its determination. These are rules of appeal. Appeal should be considered
within the four corners of the appeal. New materials cannot be
introduced at the stage of appeal.
In Seylan Bank Ltd v. Samdo Macky Sportswear (Pvt.) Ltd. and
Others (2008) 1 SLR 96, the Supreme Court held that a taxing statute
that imposes a pecuniary burden must be subject to strict construction.
The Supreme Court held:
“There is no room for intention, construction or equity about duties or
taxations. The explicit language of the Statute must be the yard stick
Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 15|16
which guides the imposition of the stamp duty and assumption and
presumptions must be strictly excluded. If the imposition of duty
upon a particular instrument is not expressly contemplated by the
simple reading of the language of the Statute, then the benefit of the
exclusion must necessarily be afforded.
The Supreme Court in the above case out frames the interpreter of taxing
statute. Statute must be interpreted with simple ready of the language of
statute. The TAC, interprets of Section 34 has named the interpretation.
Hence, the TAC has failed to apply the Supreme Court decisions
previously to the root of the case.
As explained above, the Court is answering the Questions of Law No.
1, 2, and 6 in the affirmative.
Conclusion
For the reasons adumbrated above, the questions of law are
answered as follows:
Q. N. 01. Yes
Q. N. 02. Yes
Q. N. 03. Yes
Q. N. 04. Yes

Q. N. 06. Yes

(b) Yes

Judgment CA Tax No. 124/2024 Page 16|16
As analyzed above and as the seven questions raised in the case
stated are answered in affirmative, the determination of the TAC
dated 14.05.2024 and the CGIR dated 20.03.2018 are set aside. The
Assessment is annulled and the appeal is allowed.
The Registrar is directed to forward a copy of the judgment to the Tax
appeal commission.
